tip: 'Lang niet gezien' is a fixed greeting for long time no see. It drops the verb hebben that gezien would normally need.
Naartoe adds the sense of to or toward. Nergens naartoe means nowhere to go, ergens naartoe means somewhere to go.
After waarom the clause is subordinate, so the verb goes to the end: waarom hij boos is, not waarom hij is boos.
Voorbereiden splits: the prefix voor moves to the end, so the command is bereid je voor, not voorbereid je.
Wel is the positive counter to a negative. Here geen vlees maar wel vis means no meat but yes to fish.
Starting a sentence with something other than the subject flips the order, so the verb comes first: zou ik, not ik zou.
Geen and meer wrap around the noun to mean none left: geen melk meer means no more milk.
Mogen means to be allowed. Mogen niet means not allowed, so mogen ... niet fietsen is you may not cycle.
Kloppen literally means to knock, but het klopt means that is correct. Het klopt niet means that is not right.
Regular verbs form the past with -te or -de. Koken becomes kookte, giving the simple past she cooked.
In the perfect tense split verbs put ge- in the middle: opmerken becomes opgemerkt, not geopmerkt.
For equal comparisons Dutch uses zo ... als: zo eenvoudig als means as simple as.
With al plus the present tense, wachten al een half uur means have been waiting half an hour and still are.
Zitten plus te plus an infinitive says someone is busy doing something: zit ... te werken means is sitting working.
Zich zorgen maken is a set reflexive phrase for worrying. The command keeps the je: maak je geen zorgen.
Strong verbs change their vowel in the past instead of adding an ending: zingen becomes zong, plural zongen.
The ending -je makes a small or fond version of a noun: dorp becomes dorpje, a little village.
Dutch picks a position verb by shape. Upright things staan, so the monument staat op het plein rather than is.
Hoeven means need to and shows up mainly in the negative, always paired with te: zij hoeft zich nergens ... te maken.
Bang takes voor for what you fear: bang voor spinnen means afraid of spiders.
Putting the object first flips subject and verb: een interessant boek lees ik, with lees before ik.
